title: Column Builder
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the addition chapter. An adult sees a column sum being filled in, which a child could do on squared paper. What the page is actually doing is settling the first step, which the printed six steps put before any arithmetic: arranging the numbers in the columns correctly. A child who lines the strips up by their left ends gets every column wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with adding, and on paper that is invisible until the answer is marked.

writeup.why: Put two long numbers one under the other so that every digit lands in its own column, then add them a column at a time starting from the right.
writeup.look: A ruled mat with a heading over every column, two strips of digit cards that can be slid along it, and the answer building up under the rule.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Column Builder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the columns closed against the columns the mat is ruled for, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each column total is written under the rule and the second fixed at the width of the mat. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The mat sits across the top of the working area, 800 by 300 at 207,202: ruled columns 120 wide under headings 44 tall, six of them at most, drawn from the right so that the ones column is always the rightmost and a four column mat is this same mat with its two left columns left unruled. Under the headings lie two addend rows of cells 84 tall, then a rule 6 tall running the full width of the mat, then the sum row 84 tall beneath it. An addend arrives as a strip of digit cards drawn joined into one piece, each card 96 by 76 sitting centred in its column, so a strip slides as a whole and a single digit can never be pulled out of it. A strip can be dropped anywhere along the mat, including where its right end hangs over open columns, and the heading standing over each of its digits is read out afresh as it moves, with what that digit is worth written small underneath. Check lining outlines in amber every digit that is not under its own place and names the place it is standing in instead. A column that is tapped lights the full height of both addend rows, and its total is written in green in the sum row under the rule; with the ones first control locked, only the rightmost unfinished column will light at all. There is no circle above any column on this mat and nothing ever travels leftwards across it, because no pair this tool sets takes a column past nine. The expanded strip opens beneath the mat, 1086 by 96 at 64,520, and writes each addend as its thousands, hundreds, tens and ones with plus signs 28 tall between them, every part standing under the column it came out of. The naming labels are plates 180 by 44 that land at the left end of each addend row reading addend and at the left end of the sum row reading sum, and the rule itself is drawn heavier while they are being placed. A ledge 1086 by 96 at the foot of the working area holds any strip that has not yet been given a home. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a column total or a whole sum is asked for, and on the first and fourth phases a word pad of the mat's own words, ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs, addend and sum, so that a column can be named and a row labelled with one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number being added is deep blue, the answer standing under the rule is green, a digit carried into the next column is vermilion, a rounded number is rose, the digit under discussion or the one that is missing is amber, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a carried digit by being small and by sitting above the column it is going into.
writeup.finish: The card shows the longest sum the child built, its columns still named, with the addends and the sum labelled.

phases.win: the check lining control finds nothing out of place and the empty columns stay empty
phases.does: slides the shorter strip until its ones digit stands under the ones heading
phases.goal: the addends are lined up by their right ends so each digit sits in its own column
phases.says: Line them up by their right ends. Which column does the shorter number start in?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write four thousand six and eighty two one under the other on squared paper. Which column does the eight stand in?
phases.feels: one number is shorter than the other, and the gap belongs at the left where nothing is standing
phases.hands: On squared paper write the column headings first, one to a square, and only then a five digit number with a three digit one under it, one digit to a square. Ask which square the shorter number begins in. Then write the same pair again lined up by their left ends instead and read out loud what each of its digits has become.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which column is the last digit of the shorter number standing in? Second rung, the phase's: which column does the last digit of any number belong in? Third rung: the mat is cut to three columns with one two digit strip on it and the child slides that single strip home. The word pad of column names stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: writing starts at the left everywhere else on a page, and two numbers that begin together look tidy.
wrong.move: pushes the shorter strip to the left end of the mat so that the two numbers begin under one another.
wrong.screen: the headings above the shorter strip are read out as it stands, so its leading digit is heard in the ten thousands column and the worth written under it is read out as tens of thousands; check lining then outlines every digit of that strip in amber and names the place each one is standing in. The strip is not moved for the child and nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: an empty column looks unfinished, and a square with nothing in it looks like a square that still wants something.
wrong.move: fills the shorter number's empty left columns with zeros of its own and counts them as part of it.
wrong.screen: the zeros the child wrote stay exactly where they are, drawn grey, and the strip is read out twice, once with them and once without, with the two readings written one under the other and coming to the same number; the zeros are then left standing where they were and the empty columns beside them are outlined.

phases.screen: the mat with a five digit strip in place and a three digit strip loose beside it
phases.soWhat: Line the addends up by their right ends, because every column is a place.

phases.win: the columns fill from the right and the sum stands complete under the rule
phases.does: taps the ones column, then each column to its left in turn
phases.goal: the columns are worked from the right, one at a time
phases.says: Start at the ones. Say what that column comes to before you move left.
phases.check: Why can the leftmost column not be finished before the columns to its right are done?
phases.feels: the right hand column is the only one that can be finished for certain, so it goes first
phases.hands: Write two five digit numbers on squared paper, then cover every column but the leftmost with a strip of card and try to finish that column. Uncover the ones column and ask what might still arrive from the right before the left one can be trusted.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which column is furthest to the right? Second rung, the phase's: which way does anything that will not fit in a column have to travel? Third rung: the mat is cut to two columns and the child works those two in order. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: reading and writing both run from the left, and the leftmost column is where the number seems to begin.
wrong.move: taps the leftmost column first and works rightwards, the way a number is read.
wrong.screen: every total the child wrote stays under the rule exactly where it was put. The ones first control then locks itself, the same two strips are worked again from the right with one column lighting at a time, and the two runs stand one under the other with the order of work numbered beside each column. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: the numbers are small enough to hold, and the mat looks like somewhere to show working that has already been done.
wrong.move: adds the two numbers in their head and types a whole answer without a column being touched.
wrong.screen: the mat works the columns anyway from the right, each one lighting as it is added and writing its total in green under the rule, and the child's number stands in the answer slot beside the one the mat builds; where the two part, the first column from the right that parts them is lit amber and stays lit.

phases.screen: two five digit strips lined up, with every column still blank under the rule
phases.soWhat: Adding starts at the ones and works left, because anything that spills has to move left.

phases.win: the last column on the left is worked and the mat stops, with no new rule needed
phases.does: works the same way along a longer mat and counts the steps it took
phases.goal: a six digit sum is a shorter sum with more steps on the left
phases.says: Same method, more columns. Where does it end this time?
phases.check: How many column steps does a sum of two six digit numbers take, and which of them comes first?
phases.feels: six columns and not one new thing to learn
phases.hands: Take a four digit sum the child has already worked on paper and write two more digits in front of each number to make them six digits long. Ask how many steps the new sum takes, and whether any one of those steps is a kind of step they have not done before.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many columns is the mat ruled for? Second rung, the phase's: how many of them have a total under the rule? Third rung: the mat is cut back to four columns, the child works it, and then two columns are opened at the left and the same sum is worked again. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a six digit number is the biggest thing they have written down, and big new numbers have arrived with new rules before now.
wrong.move: asks for a new rule because the numbers are longer than any they have added before.
wrong.screen: the six column sum stays where it is and the four column sum the child worked earlier is laid under it with their right ends aligned; the steps of each are counted along from the right, and each step of the longer sum is lit beside the step of the shorter one it matches, with two steps at the left end matching nothing at all.

wrong.why: five columns is what the last few sums took, and a rule with most of it written on looks like a rule that is full.
wrong.move: works five of the six columns and reads the sum as finished.
wrong.screen: the leftmost column keeps both of its digits lit with the square under the rule left empty and ringed in amber, and the sum is read out place by place from the right until the reading arrives at nothing at all. Nothing is filled in for the child.

phases.screen: the mat grown to six columns with two six digit strips on it
phases.soWhat: A longer sum is the same method with more steps, and it still starts at the ones.
phases.concept: More columns do not mean a new method

phases.win: both labels land on the right rows and the finished sum is read aloud
phases.does: labels the two strips and the answer, then reads the whole thing out
phases.goal: the parts of a written sum can be named
phases.says: Point at the addends. Now point at the sum. Say which is which.
phases.check: In a sum of your own, point at the addends and then at the sum, and say which is which.
phases.feels: the two names stay put however the numbers are swapped about
phases.hands: Point at a sum the child has finished on paper and ask for the names of its three rows. Then have them write a sum of their own and label every row before a single column is worked.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which rows are above the rule? Second rung, the phase's: what is the row under the rule called? Third rung: the mat is cut to two columns with a finished sum on it and the child lays the three labels on that. The word pad stays open and no label is ever placed for the child.

wrong.why: the three rows look alike once they are written down, and the largest number looks like the important one.
wrong.move: calls the answer under the rule an addend, because it is the largest number on the mat.
wrong.screen: the rule is drawn heavier and the two rows above it lift a little together while the word addend is written on each of them, and the row below the rule stays down and takes the word sum; the child's label stays exactly where it was put, so that the two readings can be held against each other.

wrong.why: add this to that names one number as the thing being added and the other as the thing it is added into.
wrong.move: labels only the lower strip as an addend, because only one of the numbers looks as though it is doing anything.
wrong.screen: the two strips swap rows on the mat, the columns are worked again from the right and the same total stands under the rule in green; both strips carry the word addend the whole time and neither of them is ever the one being added to.

phases.screen: a finished sum on the mat with the naming control waiting
phases.soWhat: The addends go above the rule and the sum goes under it.
phases.concept: The addends are what you add and the sum is what you get

writeup.delight: The first phase, the moment the loose strip is dragged along the mat. It does not snap anywhere and nothing is marked. As it passes each column the heading over its leading digit is read out afresh, hundreds, then thousands, then ten thousands, and the worth written small underneath grows ten times at every step, so the same three digit cards are worth hundreds in one column and tens of thousands two columns along. Slide it back and the worths shrink again the same way. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the mat stands five columns wide with a five digit strip lying home in its columns and a shorter strip loose on the ledge below it, not standing in any column at all. On the second two strips of the same length are already home and every square under the rule is blank. On the third the mat stands six columns wide with a six digit strip on each of its two rows. On the fourth a finished sum stands with its total under the rule and the naming labels waiting at the left of the mat. The running count at the top left holds the columns closed against the columns the mat is ruled for, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the loose strip, or the ones column, or the leftmost column, or the first naming label, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks for the two numbers to be lined up by their right ends. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two numbers up to six digits, with the lining check, the expanded form strip and the naming labels switched on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on lining addends up, working from the ones and adding five and six digit numbers where no column has to be carried.
voiceLines: Two numbers and a ruled mat. Line them up by their right ends.
Line them up by their right ends. Which column does the shorter number start in?
Start at the ones. Say what that column comes to before you move left.
Same method, more columns. Where does it end this time?
Point at the addends. Now point at the sum. Say which is which.
Another pair. Same mat, and the ones column still goes first.
Free play. Any two numbers, the lining check and the expanded strip as you like.
Slide them back and read the heading standing over each digit.
Every digit stood in its own column, and you worked them from the right.

observations.why: Those places are not part of that number at all.
observations.soWhat: An empty column is not an unfinished one; it is a place the number does not reach.
observations.observe: The shorter number left its left columns empty instead of filling them.

observations.why: The heading standing over a digit is what that digit is worth.
observations.soWhat: Lining up by the right ends is not tidiness, it is what makes the columns true.
observations.observe: Pushing the short strip one column to the left made every digit in it worth ten times as much.

observations.why: No pair here takes a column past nine, so nothing ever has to move to the left.
observations.soWhat: That is exactly what changes the moment a column does pass nine, which is the next mount's whole job.
observations.observe: Nothing left any column on this mat, so the sum came out as long as the longer addend.

observations.why: The ones column is the only column that nothing can ever arrive into.
observations.soWhat: The order of work is part of the method, not a matter of taste.
observations.observe: The columns were worked from the right and the sum filled from the right.

observations.why: A column total is the thousands, hundreds, tens and ones added apart from one another.
observations.soWhat: The expanded form is the column sum laid out sideways.
observations.observe: The expanded strip and the mat held the same sum written two ways.

source_tool.description: A ruled mat fills the stage with one column for each place and a heading over every column. Two numbers arrive as strips of digit cards, and the child slides each strip along the mat until it sits where it belongs. The mat accepts any position, so a strip can be pushed left until its right end hangs over open columns, and the headings above the digits change as it moves, so the child can read that the ones digit is now standing in the hundreds column. A check lining control lights every digit that is not under its own place. Once the strips are settled, the columns are worked one at a time from the right, each lighting as it is added, and the running sum builds up under the rule. Nothing in this tool carries: every pair it sets keeps each column at nine or less, so the lining up and the order of working are the only two things that can go wrong. An expanded form strip can be opened beneath the mat, which writes each number as its thousands and hundreds and tens and ones so that the column mat and the expanded sum can be read against each other. A naming control labels the two strips as the addends and the answer under the rule as the sum.
source_tool.art_direction: Two digit strips on a ruled mat / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that tie themselves together, a rule under the last addend, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A sum is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the addends stacked with their right ends aligned, and a horizontal rule between the last addend and the sum. A bare row of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach adding.
A carried digit is always drawn small, above the column it is being added into, never in the margin and never below the rule.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number being added is deep blue, the sum under the rule is green, and a digit carried into the next column is vermilion, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A rounded number and any estimated sum are rose, so an estimate is told apart from an exact answer before either is read. The digit under discussion, which is usually the one that is missing, is amber. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a carry is told apart by being small and sitting above its column before it is told apart by its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Slide them back and read the heading standing over each digit.
voice.onNext: Another pair. Same mat, and the ones column still goes first.
voice.opening: Two numbers and a ruled mat. Line them up by their right ends.
voice.onFinish: Every digit stood in its own column, and you worked them from the right.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any two numbers, the lining check and the expanded strip as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: More columns do not mean a new method
The addends are what you add and the sum is what you get

placement.where: Straight after the first column sum has been set out on squared paper by hand, and before the second one. The tool is what lets a wrong lining up be seen rather than marked.

answer_key.rule: Line the addends up by their right ends, so that each digit stands in the column of its own place. A shorter addend leaves its left columns empty rather than filled. Add the ones column first and work leftwards, one column at a time, writing each total under the rule. The numbers being added are the addends and the answer under the rule is the sum.
answer_key.wrong: The strips slide back out and are laid down again one column at a time, with the heading over each digit read aloud as it lands. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Line the two numbers up by their right ends, so the 2 of 362 sits under the 5 of 43,215.
362 is three hundred sixty-two, so its 3 stands in the hundreds column.
The ten thousands and thousands columns of the shorter number stay empty, and the sum is 43,577.
items.answer: The hundreds column, and the sum is 43,577
items.question: Set out 43,215 + 362 on a column mat. Which column does the 3 of 362 stand in, and what is the sum?
items.checkpoint: Lining up by the right ends puts every digit in the column of its own place.
items.misconception: Pushing 362 under the left of 43,215 so its 3 lands in the ten thousands column.

steps: Then the tens, 3 + 4 = 7, then the hundreds, 4 + 2 = 6.
Then the thousands, 5 + 3 = 8, and the ten thousands, 2 + 1 = 3, giving 38,677.
items.answer: The ones column, which comes to 7, and the sum is 38,677
items.question: Add 25,431 and 13,246, and say which column you finish first and what it comes to.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: slides each addend left or right along the column mat
lights every digit that is not standing under its own place
reads the column name over whichever digit is touched
works the lit column and writes its total under the rule
locks the working order so the rightmost column lights first
writes each addend as its thousands, hundreds, tens and ones
labels the two strips as the addends and the answer as the sum

teaching_notes: Set the first sum out on squared paper by hand before the tool is opened, one digit to a square, and write the column headings in before any digit goes in. Then use the tool to do the thing paper cannot: push a strip out of line on purpose and ask what each digit is now worth. A child who has seen the headings change over a digit does not line numbers up by their left ends again. Keep the ones first control locked for the first few sums and make them say each column total out loud before the next one lights. Open the expanded strip once the columns are settled, so the expanded form is read as the same sum written sideways rather than as a separate exercise. Use the naming control every time and insist on the words: the addends are what you add, the sum is what you get. Those two words carry the rest of the chapter, and the vocabulary work near the end of the printed chapter asks for them back.
generation_prompt: Build a column addition tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A ruled mat of place value columns, four to six of them, with a named heading over each column. Two addends appear as strips of digit cards that can be dragged horizontally along the mat and dropped in any column position, with the heading above each digit updating live as the strip moves. A check lining control outlines every digit that is not standing under its own place and names the place it is standing in instead. Columns are worked by tapping, in right to left order when the ones first control is locked, each tapped column lighting and writing its total under a horizontal rule. Every pair the tool sets keeps each column at nine or less, so no carry is ever drawn here. An expanded form strip opens beneath the mat and writes each addend as a sum of its thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, aligned with the columns above it. A naming control drops labels reading addend on each strip and sum on the answer row. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Slide each number along the mat until its right end is in the ones column. Press check lining to see whether every digit is under its own heading. Then tap the ones column and work leftwards, one column at a time, until the sum is finished. Name the addends and the sum before you leave.
